newsitem.title: UK: Minor metals - Bismuth extends gains, eyes $4.00.
newsitem.headline: Minor metals - Bismuth extends gains, eyes $4.00.

text.p: Waves of merchant covering extended bismuth gains over the past week and several traders expect prices to mount an attack on $4.00 a pound near-term.
Elsewhere in a buoyant minor metal sector, cadmium was starting to boil, while cobalt against the backdrop of short supply, was steadfast and eyeing higher levels.
A lack of Peruvian and Mexican stocks and talk of shipment delays from major producer China, where sellers were holding out for higher prices, helped to drive bismuth higher.
"There is little stock on the ground and the Chinese are holding back in anticipation of higher prices," one European trader commented.
North America is one of the largest consumers of the metal which can be used in shot gun pellets and pharmaceuticals.

One London trader said that consumers in the region have been caught short and are finding it hard to cover their requirements. "They believed there was enough stock around but are now fighting for any available material,' the trader said.

Traders noted that the U.S. Defense National Stockpile Center sold 233,752 pounds of bismuth recently. The sale exhausts the quantify of bismuth for sale in the current fiscal year which ends Sept 30.

Cadmium prices heated up as traders and merchants eyed low producer and consumer stocks. One trader suggested that cadmium had the potential to reach one dollar a pound over the coming weeks and possibly $1.50.
Talk continued to circulate that there were two large shorts in the cadmium market totalling around 300 tonnes which would have to be covered in the next two months.
One trader said that China and India were building new battery facilities which will produce nickel/cadmium units.

Low global stocks underpinned cobalt which was looking to make a fresh upside advance in the coming weeks. Robust demand from super-alloy, battery, catalyst and magnet industries should help to keep inventories at a low levels, traders said.

Production at Zambia's ZCCM continues to fall, sources close to the producer said. The old and nearly exhausted Nchanga open pit is experiencing production problems while total output from all of ZCCM's facilities are expected to fall to around 250 tonnes in May from levels of 366 tonnes seen in January.
One London trader believed that Zambia continues to air freight cobalt to customers in Europe but this may be halted at the end of this month, causing a hiatus in the supply pipeline.

Another informed source said that Zaire's Gecamines is not exporting any material at present. "No Zairian material is finding its way into Europe which is suffering from low stock levels," the source said.
In early May Gecamines Secretary-General Mutombo told Reuters that the cobalt and copper mines in the Shaba region were working normally.
Major north American produces are said to be sold out.

Traders noted comments made by Jacques Bacardats chief executive officer at speed steel producer Erasteel that high cobalt prices are causing consumer concern. But Bacardats, who was talking to Reuters during a nickel industry meeting organised by Erasteel's holding group Eramet, expected a price reversal in the third quarter of 1997.

He said the price increases were due to civil war in Zaire and the suspension of U.S. stockpile cobalt sales due to a legal dispute between the U.S. Defense Logistics Agency (DLA) and Minor Metals Inc.
"The two factors have been enough to tip the balance after steady conditions in early 1997," Badardats said.
"The price could increase further in the coming weeks but we hope it will return to normal after that."
Traders believe the price of the minor metal go to $27 or $30 before the Zairian crisis is resolved.
Magnesium probed higher despite talk of Russian stockpile offers.
Traders said demand from magnesium is turning after months of neglect, noting a slight decline in Chinese exports.
Elsewhere rhodium firmed on investment fund and physical interest.
Gallium spiked higher on news that Rhone-Poulenc Australia will next month suspend gallium extraction at its Pinjarra facility.
A lack of Chinese material underpinned molybdendum, while titanium stirred on consumer enquiry.
